title: CS 6501: Distributed Consensus & Raft Protocol
summary: This lecture covers the fundamental problems of distributed consensus in asynchronous networks with crash-stop failure models. We dissect Paxos complexity, introduce the Raft algorithm's leader election, log replication, and safety invariants, followed by network partitioning splits-brain mitigation.

slides.title: Course Intro & The Consensus Problem
slides.excerpt: Why is consensus hard? In distributed systems with unreliable networks, nodes must agree on state transitions despite message loss and node crashes.

slides.title: FLP Impossibility & Quorums
slides.excerpt: Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) theorem proves no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee liveness in an asynchronous system with even 1 crash.

slides.title: Raft Architecture: 3 Roles & Terms
slides.excerpt: Nodes exist in one of three states: Follower, Candidate, or Leader. Time is divided into arbitrary terms identified with monotonic integers.

slides.title: Leader Election & Heartbeat Timers
slides.excerpt: Randomized election timeouts (150ms-300ms) prevent split votes. A candidate wins if it receives votes from a majority (N/2 + 1) of the cluster.

slides.title: Log Replication & Commit Invariants
slides.excerpt: The leader receives client commands, appends them to its log, and sends AppendEntries RPCs. An entry is committed once replicated across a majority.

slides.title: Safety Rules & Joint Consensus Reconfiguration
slides.excerpt: Election Safety: at most one leader per term. Leader Append-Only: leader never overwrites or truncates its own log entries.

flashcards.front: What are the 3 states a node can assume in the Raft consensus protocol?
How does Raft mitigate split-vote stalemates during leader election?
flashcards.back: By using randomized election timeouts (e.g., between 150ms and 300ms) so one node times out first and requests votes.

flashcards.front: What condition must be satisfied for a log entry to be considered committed?
flashcards.back: The leader must successfully replicate the log entry to a strict majority of nodes (quorum: ⌊N/2⌋ + 1) in the current term.

flashcards.front: What is the Raft Log Matching Property?
flashcards.back: If two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, they are identical in all entries up through the given index.

quiz.question: What is the primary mechanism Raft uses to prevent multiple candidates from splitting votes indefinitely?
options: Priority queues based on node IP addresses
Randomized election timeouts on each node
quiz.explanation: Randomized election timeouts ensure nodes wake up at staggered intervals, allowing one candidate to initiate election and collect quorum before competitors.

quiz.question: In a 5-node Raft cluster, what is the minimum quorum size required to elect a leader or commit an entry?
quiz.explanation: Quorum is calculated as floor(N/2) + 1. For N=5, floor(5/2)+1 = 3 nodes.

title: CS 7641: Transformer Architectures & Self-Attention Mechanics
summary: Detailed exploration of the Transformer architecture from Attention Is All You Need. Mathematical derivation of Scaled Dot-Product Attention, Multi-Head projections, Positional Encoding strategies (Sinusoidal vs RoPE), and LayerNorm dynamics.

slides.title: From RNNs & LSTMs to Attention
slides.excerpt: Recurrent networks suffer from vanishing gradients across long sequences and cannot be easily parallelized across sequence length dimensions.

slides.title: Scaled Dot-Product Attention Derivation
slides.excerpt: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( (Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k) ) * V. The scaling factor 1/sqrt(d_k) prevents large dot-products from pushing softmax into vanishing gradients.

slides.title: Multi-Head Attention Projections
slides.excerpt: Multi-head attention projects Queries, Keys, and Values into h different subspaces, allowing the model to jointly attend to information at different positions.

slides.title: Positional Encodings: Fixed vs Rotary
slides.excerpt: Transformers possess no inherent recurrence or convolution; positional information is injected via sinusoidal frequency vectors or Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE).

flashcards.front: Why is the dot product scaled by 1/√d_k in self-attention?
flashcards.back: For large values of d_k, dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing softmax into vanishing gradient regions.

flashcards.front: What is the computational complexity of standard self-attention for sequence length N and dimension d?
flashcards.back: O(N² · d) time and O(N²) memory complexity for the attention matrix.

quiz.question: What is the primary reason for dividing by √d_k in Scaled Dot-Product Attention?
options: To prevent vanishing softmax gradients caused by large dot-product magnitudes
To reduce computational complexity from O(N^2) to O(N log N)
To ensure rotational invariance in embedding space
quiz.explanation: When d_k is large, dot products have higher variance, pushing softmax outputs toward 0 or 1 where gradients are near zero.
